quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter l: a tall straight line from the top line down to the baseline.
quests.question: l
quests.hint: Start at the top line and pull straight down. Stop on the baseline. Keep the line upright, not leaning.
quests.explanation: Lowercase l is a tall stem. Because it reaches the top line, it is called an ascender, and it is taller than letters like a or c.
quests.funFact: In some fonts the capital I and the lowercase l look almost identical, so writers need to be careful.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter i: a short stem from the middle line, then a dot above it.
quests.question: i
quests.hint: Start at the middle line, pull down to the baseline, then lift your pen and put a dot right above it.
quests.explanation: Lowercase i is short: its top is at the middle line. Its dot sits above the stem, not off to one side.
quests.funFact: The lowercase i got its dot in the Middle Ages, to make it stand out among the tall strokes of other letters.

quests.instruction: Write i and l next to each other. One is short with a dot, the other is tall.
quests.question: i l
quests.hint: Write i first, starting at the middle line. Then write l, starting at the top line.
quests.explanation: Writing a short letter beside a tall one makes you feel the difference in height, which matters in every word.
quests.funFact: The word 'minuscule', meaning very small, comes from the same Latin word as our lowercase letters.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter t: a tall-ish stem with a short bar across it.
quests.question: t
quests.hint: Start a little below the top line, pull straight down, then cross it with a short bar at the middle line.
quests.explanation: Lowercase t is taller than a but shorter than l. The crossbar sits at the middle line, level with the tops of small letters.
quests.funFact: A part of a letter that rises above the main body, like the top of a t, is called an ascender.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter j: a short stem that drops below the line with a hook, and a dot above it.
quests.question: j
quests.hint: Start at the middle line like i, but keep pulling down past the baseline, then flick a hook to the left. Add the dot last.
quests.explanation: The part of j under the baseline is called a descender. The hook keeps the letter from looking like a plain i.
quests.funFact: The letter j began as a long, curly way of writing the letter i.

quests.instruction: Write t, j, i in a row. Pay attention to the cross and the dots.
quests.question: t j i
quests.hint: Cross the t at the middle line. Put the dots on j and i directly above their stems.
quests.explanation: Crosses and dots are small details that you add last. Placing them well makes writing much easier to read.
quests.funFact: Around the year 800, scribes at the court of Charlemagne developed a clear style called Carolingian minuscule, an ancestor of our lowercase letters.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter u: down, curve at the bottom, up, and then a straight line down.
quests.question: u
quests.hint: Start at the middle line and pull down. Curve at the bottom, go up to the middle line, then pull straight down to the baseline.
quests.explanation: Lowercase u has a round bottom and a stem on its right. The curve is on the left and the stem makes the second side.
quests.funFact: The letter u can sound different in 'cup', 'put' and 'unit'.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter y: two strokes, with a tail below the line.
quests.question: y
quests.hint: Slant down to the right from the middle line. Then start at the top right and slant down-left, going below the baseline.
quests.explanation: Lowercase y has two strokes that meet and a tail that drops below the baseline. The tail makes it a descender.
quests.funFact: In old English books, 'ye' was often used for 'the', because the old letter thorn looked like a y.

quests.instruction: Write u and y side by side. Both are small letters, but one has a tail.
quests.question: u y
quests.hint: Write u, resting on the baseline. Then y, which also reaches the middle line at the top but drops a tail underneath.
quests.explanation: Letters can be the same height on top and different at the bottom. The tail of y is part of its shape.
quests.funFact: About one person in ten is left-handed.

quests.instruction: From memory, write l, i and t.
quests.question: l i t
quests.hint: Remember heights: l starts at the top line, t starts a little below it, and the top of i is at the middle line.
quests.explanation: These letters are all stems, only their heights and extra marks differ. Remember height first, details second.
quests.funFact: A fountain pen holds ink inside and feeds it to the tip as you write.

quests.instruction: Write the two letters that have dots: i and j.
quests.question: i j
quests.hint: Write the stems first, then the dots. Dots should sit above the stems, not leaning away.
quests.explanation: Stem first, dot last is a good routine. Dots are the last step so you don't lose your place.
quests.funFact: The sepia-brown ink once made from cuttlefish was used for writing and drawing.

quests.instruction: Write l, t, j, i in order. Make the heights different on purpose.
quests.question: l t j i
quests.hint: Tall l, a bit shorter t, small j with a tail, small i. Say 'tall, medium, tail, small' as you go.
quests.explanation: Changing height on purpose is a key skill. Words need tall, short and tail letters in the right places.
quests.funFact: Children long ago often practiced writing on small slate boards using chalk.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter c: a small open curve that fits between the middle line and the baseline.
quests.question: c
quests.hint: Start near the top right of the space, curve left and down, then stop at the bottom right. Leave it open.
quests.explanation: Lowercase c is a small version of the capital curve. It sits entirely between the middle line and the baseline.
quests.funFact: In Italian, the letter c before e or i is pronounced like 'ch', as in 'ciao'.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter o: a small closed circle, as tall as the c.
quests.question: o
quests.hint: Start at the top and go left, around the bottom and up. Close the circle neatly at the top.
quests.explanation: Lowercase o is a small circle whose height matches c. Closing it neatly shows control.
quests.funFact: People often say 'oh' for zero when reading numbers aloud, as in 'oh-seven'.

quests.instruction: Write c and o together. Both should be exactly the same height.
quests.question: c o
quests.hint: Check that the tops of c and o touch the middle line and that the bottoms sit on the baseline.
quests.explanation: Letters that fit between the middle line and the baseline are called x-height letters, because they are as tall as the letter x.
quests.funFact: The 'x-height' of a font is measured on the letter x, because its top and bottom are flat.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter a: a small circle with a short stem on its right.
quests.question: a
quests.hint: Make a small c-shaped circle from the top. Then pull a short line down on the right side, touching the circle.
quests.explanation: Lowercase a is a circle plus a stem. The stem must touch the circle so the shape stays closed.
quests.funFact: In many printed books, the letter a looks different from the handwritten form, with an extra curve at the top.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter d: draw an a-style circle, then a tall stem on the right.
quests.question: d
quests.hint: Make the circle first. Then, from the top line, pull a tall line down on the right side to the baseline.
quests.explanation: d is a circle with a tall stem. The stem is an ascender, so it must reach the top line, unlike the short stem of a.
quests.funFact: In old British money, the letter d stood for 'penny', from the Latin word 'denarius'.

quests.instruction: Write a and d together. See how the stem is short on one and tall on the other.
quests.question: a d
quests.hint: For a, the stem is short: it starts at the middle line. For d, the stem starts all the way up at the top line.
quests.explanation: Same circle, different stem height. This is why careful height control matters to readability.
quests.funFact: Handwriting styles taught in schools differ from country to country.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter g: draw a circle, then a stem that drops below the baseline with a hook.
quests.question: g
quests.hint: Make a small circle. Then pull a line down on the right, past the baseline, and curve to the left at the bottom.
quests.explanation: Lowercase g has a circle on the line and a descender below it. The hook on g curves left.
quests.funFact: In some printed fonts the letter g has a loop at the bottom, like a pair of spectacles.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter q: a circle with a stem on the right that goes below the line, with no hook.
quests.question: q
quests.hint: Make the circle. Then pull a straight stem down the right side, past the baseline, and stop.
quests.explanation: q looks like g without the hook. The straight tail is what makes it q.
quests.funFact: The word 'queue' is spelled with q, u, e, u, e, but you only say the 'q' sound, like 'cue'.

quests.instruction: Write g and q next to each other. Check which tail has a hook and which one is straight.
quests.question: g q
quests.hint: g has a hook that turns left, q has a straight tail. Both tails go below the baseline.
quests.explanation: These two are easy to mix up. Remember: g hooks, q does not.
quests.funFact: Quill pens were made from the large wing feathers of birds such as geese.

quests.instruction: From memory, write c, o and a in a row.
quests.question: c o a
quests.hint: All three start at the top and go to the left. Close o, leave c open, and add a stem to a.
quests.explanation: Round letters share the same start. Remembering the path helps you write all three correctly.
quests.funFact: A fountain pen needs ink, while a ballpoint pen has a tiny ball at its tip that rolls the ink onto the paper.

quests.instruction: Write d, g and q from memory. Each has a circle and a stem.
quests.question: d g q
quests.hint: Draw the circle first. d has a tall stem. g has a stem that hooks below. q has a straight tail below.
quests.explanation: Three letters made from one shape with three different stems. Notice how the stem alone changes the letter.
quests.funFact: Chalkboards were used in schools in the early 1800s.

quests.instruction: Write o, c, a, d, g and q in a row, keeping the circles the same size.
quests.question: o c a d g q
quests.correctAnswer: o c a d g q
quests.hint: Plan the row first. Make every circle the same size as the first o. Stems go up or down from the circles.
quests.explanation: Six letters with circles is a good test. All circles should be the same size and sit on the baseline.
quests.funFact: Rubber erasers were named 'rubbers' in English because they were used to rub out pencil marks.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter h: a tall stem, then an arch that sits on the middle line.
quests.question: h
quests.hint: Pull straight down from the top line. Go back up the stem halfway, then arch over and down to the baseline.
quests.explanation: h is a tall stem with a hump. Starting the arch partway up the stem makes it look neat and joined.
quests.funFact: In Spanish, the letter h is almost always silent.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter n: a short stem, then an arch.
quests.question: n
quests.hint: n is h's shorter sister: begin at the middle line, trace down, go back up a little and make the arch.
quests.explanation: n is h without the tall stem. Remember that the arch starts from the stem, not from the top.
quests.funFact: Arches are very strong shapes and have been used in buildings for thousands of years.

quests.instruction: Write h and n side by side. Make both arches the same size.
quests.question: h n
quests.hint: Look at the arch of h, then copy exactly the same arch for n. Only the stems differ in height.
quests.explanation: Writers call the arch of letters like h, n and m the shoulder. Keeping shoulders the same size keeps writing even.
quests.funFact: Handwriting experts say that the shape of arches can differ between writers.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter m: a stem, then two arches in a row.
quests.question: m
quests.hint: Pull down from the middle line. Go back up the stem a little, then make one arch, and another arch right beside it.
quests.explanation: m is a stem with two arches. Both arches should be the same size, and their right sides should touch the baseline.
quests.funFact: M is also a Roman numeral and stands for 1,000.

quests.instruction: Write the lowercase letter r: a short stem with a small curve at the top.
quests.question: r
quests.hint: Pull down from the middle line. Go back up the stem a little and curve out to the right, like a tiny arch.
quests.explanation: r is a short stem plus a half arch. It is small, and the curve ends well before the baseline.
quests.funFact: In Spanish and Italian, the letter r can be rolled with the tongue.

quests.instruction: Write m, r and n in a row. All three have arches.
quests.question: m r n
quests.hint: m has two arches, n has one, r has half an arch. Space them evenly.
quests.explanation: Telling arches apart: two, one, and a half. Count them as you write.
quests.funFact: Italic handwriting developed in Italy in the 1400s.
